recode_values(

  c(1, 2, 3) ~ "Secondary school or less",
  c(4, 5, 6) ~ "Bachelor degree or higher",

notes: The study records only the MEAN of the two parents on a 6-level scale (1 elementary, 2 technical school, 3 high school, 4 degree/college, 5 master's/university, 6 doctoral/postgraduate), not the higher of the two, so the schema's `highest across parents` cannot be read off directly. `ceiling()` recovers the higher parent's level whenever the two are within one step, and otherwise understates it. Validated at T2, where the study also releases the two parents separately: after the collapse to three bands, ceiling(mean) agrees with pmax(respondent, spouse) for 105 of 108 rows and errs downwards in the other 3. The T2-only pair is deliberately not used, so the method does not change between waves. The scale has no non-degree tertiary level, so nothing maps to Post-secondary. Highly educated sample: 86% land in the top band at T1.

The T2 spouse-education item is left blank for 11 of 108 respondents (the codebook reads `if she/he has`), and 9 of those 11 live in two-person households, which reads as single-parent. But the item is asked at T2 only, a blank could equally be a non-response, and nothing anywhere distinguishes two biological/adoptive parents from a step family, so the three-way schema category cannot be built.

The study asked banded items, not open numeric entry: how often the child uses a smartphone/tablet (8 frequency bands) and how long a typical session lasts (7 duration bands), separately per device. The authors multiplied the band midpoints to get minutes per day (doi:10.3390/su14148845, Section 2.2.1 and Appendix A), which is why the contributed variable takes 102 distinct fractional values despite a categorical origin.
